subject: Question about spatial multispecies single season model

messages.author: 1fc8279e9cddc6a6
messages.subject: Question about spatial multispecies single season model
parts:
Hello,
First off thank you again for this google group, I have used it a lot the last year! I have been running a single-season, multi-species occupancy model (27 sites, 3 repeat surveys, 14 species; some species are rare, with only a few detections, 5 covariates in the model) using msPGOcc(). The overall goal is to examine how community and trophic guild (I do this analysis using postHocLM function) occupancy differ with these covariates. The model performed well (traceplots converged, high ESS, rhat less than 1.1, checked values with ppcOcc). I checked for spatial autocorrelation using a join-count statistic and found autocorrelation for several species (over half). I was therefore thinking to run a spatial model to help account for this. I have several questions related to this.

Based on what I read in the google group and documentation for the package, I think the function I want to use is sfMsPGOcc (Q1) is that correct?), so I went ahead and ran a model using 2 factors based on # of species I have. This model performed well too, with similar results in the model diagnostics and similar occupancy effects (MCMC plots, means etc). The WAIC of the spatial model was 20 units lower than that of the non-spatial model.

Q3) Is there a different way I should be checking for spatial auto-correlation in models such as this? I tried to look at the residuals and moran's I, but I am not sure my code is correct. If it is then the spatial model has a lower I than the non-spatial.
Q4) At this point, is this enough reason to present the spatial results instead?
Q5) If I am not noticing much change in the occupancy effects, what is the spatial modeling adding? Or is this a sign it is not adding any info to the model/the model cannot support a spatial term due to sample size, rare detections, etc. 
Q6) At this point, if I want to use this data for further analyses, is there anything else I need to check before doing that? For example before using this new spatial model in the post Hoc LM 

Thank you again, apologies for the long email!


I am pasting my spatial model code below:
set.seed(123)

formula_all <- ~ Distance_to_Edge + Forest_Type + Hololens_Measure +
  Canopy_Cover_Percentage + Distance_to_National_Park


# Spatial Factor Model: All Variables --------------------------------------
batch.length <- 25
n.batch <- 1000   # 25 * 1000 = 25,000 total samples, same as used in original non-spatial

model_1_sp <- sfMsPGOcc(
  occ.formula = formula_all,
  det.formula = ~ 1,
  data = array_list,
  n.factors = 2,              # number of latent spatial factors, 2 for now cut to 1 if needed
  cov.model = "exponential",
  NNGP = TRUE,
  n.neighbors = 15,
  tuning = list(phi = 1),     # starting tuning value for the spatial decay
  n.batch = n.batch,
  batch.length = batch.length,
  n.burn = 5000,
  n.thin = 5,
  n.chains = 5,
  n.omp.threads = 1,
  n.report = 100,
  verbose = TRUE
)

messages.author: 0b274a0ee3490d75
messages.subject: Re: Question about spatial multispecies single season model
parts:
Hi Annie, 

Thanks for the note. Responses to each of your questions below:
  1. Yes, sfMsPGOcc is the function I would recommend using to fit a multi-species spatial occupancy model. 
  2. Using a join count statistic for testing for spatial autocorrelation is a good approach. There is not currently a direct built-in way in spOccupancy to asses residual spatial autocorrelation, so I don't have a better alternative for this. 
  3. With only 27 spatial locations, you have very little information to estimate any of the spatial parameters in the model. What is likely happening is that the estimates of the spatial variance and decay parameter are being almost entirely informed by the priors, and so there is likely large uncertainty in these estimates. What is also likely to happen is that your credible intervals will be overly conservative (i.e., too large), although this in some ways depends on the scale of the spatial autocorrelation relative to the area sampled by your data points (and the space between data points). Given you only have 27 spatial locations, I would probably recommend you move forward with the nonspatial model and acknowledge that residual spatial autocorrelation could be present. By ignoring residual spatial autocorrelation, the main impacts (given your objectives) is that credible intervals on the covariate effects may be too precise (i.e., overly confident), and so you may be underestimating the amount of uncertainty in those effects. However, given the downsides of fitting a spatial model with such few spatial locations, I think that is something you will just have to acknowledge and take into consideration when interpreting any effects that appear marginally "significant". 
  4. See previous point. The spatial model won't add much here given that you only have 27 locations and could lead to overly conservative credible intervals. 
  5. Not that I can think of, but as I mentioned above, I would recommend using the nonspatial model for your subsequent guild assessments. 
Hope that helps!

Jeff
